title: Preserve IR variable identity and reserve wrapper-owned names in generated signatures
applies_when: A host wrapper, launcher, cache or dynamic-shape binding turns scalar Var name_hint values into Python/C++ parameter names, especially distinct Vars with the same hint or names such as stream, kernels and device_id.
lesson: A printable name_hint is not IR variable identity or a unique generated identifier. Inspect the real Var objects and compile generated host source with both same-hint and distinct-name controls. Also test names reserved by each backend's wrapper. Removing a repeated entry loses a positional input; renaming only the declaration can leave expression, shape, descriptor and device-call references pointing at another input. Any repair needs consistent identity-based mapping across these uses while reserving wrapper-owned names, rather than a string-level deduplication. Prefer a native lowering plus the complete wrapper constructor where available.
avoid_when: The demonstrated failure is generated Python signature compilation, not a GPU numerical or launch qualification. Source-generation fixtures alone do not establish actual lowering reachability. Backend-specific reserved names differ. The public reproduction used release 0.1.15 native dependencies and byte-identical pinned current-main wrapper Python, not a full current-main native rebuild. Do not reject all same-hint IR, assume a naming repair is complete, or copy its identifiers into other backends without matching their contracts.

evidence.note: Native Var/PrimFunc and Python compiler checks: 10 source-generation cases cover duplicate n, distinct n/m and stream/kernels/device_id collisions with backend-specific passing controls. An additional real TIR-lowering/full-NVRTC-constructor pair reproduces the duplicate signature versus a valid control. CUDA hidden; no generated module execution, binary compilation or numerical GPU test.
Scalar arguments use raw param.name; dynamic-symbol name deduplication is separate. The generated call also adds stream and device_id, so only checking distinct user names is insufficient.
NVRTC prepends kernels, appends the implicit stream argument, and collects raw scalar names. The same string can collide with wrapper state even when user scalar names are distinct.
